data.title: Hello, I'm Maya.
data.intro: I just finished a degree in human-computer interaction. I like small problems that are easy to explain and hard to get right.

children.text: I grew up in a family that ran a small print shop, so I learned early that a good sign or form saves people time. That is what drew me to interaction design. At university I moved from sketching on paper to building working prototypes, and I enjoy both.

Over four years I worked on three course projects, two team projects and a handful of personal ones. I spent a summer as a UX intern in a small studio, and I work two evenings a week at the university library help desk.
I start by asking people what they are trying to do. Then I make something rough, show it, and change it. I write things down so the team can follow what I decided and why.
A junior UX, product design or front-end role in a small team. I would like a mentor, real users to talk to, and the chance to ship something within my first few months.
Maya Linden is a fictional person and the portrait on this site is AI-generated for the theme. If you use the theme for your own site, replace the photo, name and every detail in the admin.

data.title: About this site
data.intro: How the sample site is built and what is made up.

children.text: This is a sample site for an early-career resume. The name, university, employers and projects are fictional. Phone numbers use the 555-01xx range and email addresses use the .example domain.
The text is set in Newsreader and Inter. The handwritten notes use Zeyada. All fonts are free and self-hosted. The portrait and project images are AI-generated for the theme.

data.title: Leafly
data.summary: A minimal plant care app for healthier homes.
data.problem: My flatmates and I kept losing houseplants. Every care app I tried asked for a long setup and then sent reminders for plants we no longer owned. I wanted something that does one job: tell you which plant needs water today.
data.built:
Designed a home screen with three prompts only: water, light and thrive.
Built the app in React Native with plants stored on the phone, no account needed.
Tested a paper version with four flatmates before writing any code.
Added a weekly view after two testers asked what they had missed.
data.learned: Cutting features was harder than adding them. My first design had a plant encyclopedia and nobody opened it. I also learned how to ship a small app to a real device and fix the bugs people actually hit.
data.gallery:
/images/leafly-phone.webp | The home screen with the three daily prompts
/images/leafly-plant.webp | A test plant used in the early photo diary

data.title: Roam
data.summary: A travel journal for mindful explorers.
data.problem: The brief for my interaction design studio was to redesign a travel website for people who plan slowly. Most travel sites push deals and countdown timers, which is the opposite of what the people I interviewed wanted.
data.built:
Interviewed five friends and family members about how they plan and remember trips.
Designed a journal-style layout where photos come first and booking links come last.
Built a three-page prototype in Astro and presented it to the class.
data.learned: Interview notes are only useful if you write them up the same day. I also learned to ask people to show me their last trip photos instead of describing them.
data.gallery: /images/roam-screen.webp | The landing screen of the prototype

data.title: NextStep
data.role: Researcher and front-end developer, team of four
data.problem: Four of us in a final-year module were each using a different planner, and deadlines kept slipping through. We set out to build one shared place for a student to plan a term: a week view, a reading list and a short reflection at the end of each week.
data.built:
Ran a survey of 31 classmates and summarised it for the team in one page.
Built the week view and the reflection form in TypeScript.
Wrote the user test script and ran three of the five test sessions.
Presented the project to the module lead with the rest of the team.
data.learned: Working in a team of four taught me to agree on small tasks and write them down. We had two weeks where we all worked on the same screen and overwrote each other's files, and after that we split the work by page.
data.gallery:
/images/nextstep-notebook.webp | The paper planner we started from
/images/nextstep-mug.webp | The team's weekly reflection prompt

data.title: Pocket Syllabus
data.summary: A one-page view of every module, deadline and reading for the term.
data.problem: Module handbooks are long PDFs. In a short survey of my course group, 9 of 12 people said they only opened theirs twice a term. The project asked: what is the smallest useful version of a syllabus?
data.built:
Collected the handbooks for six modules and listed every deadline in one spreadsheet.
Sketched four layouts on paper and tested them with eight classmates.
Made a clickable Figma prototype of the layout most people picked.
data.learned: People trust a page they can print. The paper version was used more than the screen version, which I did not expect.
data.gallery: /images/desk-notebook.webp | A notebook page from the paper testing round

data.title: Quiet Hours
data.summary: A small timer that blocks distractions during a study session.
data.tools:
JavaScript
CSS
A browser extension manifest
data.problem: I study better in 50-minute blocks, but I kept opening other tabs. I wanted a timer that sits quietly in the browser and asks before it lets me leave.
data.built:
Built a browser extension with a timer, a break reminder and a short list of sites to pause.
Wrote a one-page guide for the three friends who tried it.
Fixed a bug where the timer kept running after the laptop went to sleep.
data.learned: I learned how browser extensions are packaged and why small bugs, like the sleep one, matter more than new features.
data.gallery: /images/nextstep-mug.webp | The mug on my desk that gave the project its name

data.title: Greenway Walks
data.summary: A map of short, step-free walks around campus.
data.problem: A classmate who uses a wheelchair told us that campus maps show buildings but not which paths are step-free or well lit. Our group set out to map ten short walks with that information.
data.built:
Walked and timed ten routes with our classmate and noted gradients, surfaces and lighting.
Designed a printable map and a phone view with the same information.
Shared the map with the student union for feedback.
data.learned: Asking the person who needs the thing is faster than guessing. We changed three routes after one walk.
data.gallery: /images/desk-leaves.webp | The courtyard route in late afternoon
